overview: This file consists of a one-page Department of State list-of-papers sheet indexing correspondence from August 1940 through March 1941 about foreign-exchange controls in the Kwantung Leased Territory. The indexed papers concern the American Consulate at Dairen’s difficulty converting or accepting local currency, particularly its refusal to issue a consular bill of health to the SAN PEDRO MARU before the vessel sailed for Los Angeles. The entries also record consultations with Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, the Japanese Foreign Minister, the Department of State, and the Public Health Service over whether the consul acted properly and whether the dispute represented a deliberate test of American consular practice.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers concerning exchange controls in the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.about: An index identifies correspondence concerning Kwantung foreign-exchange regulations and the Dairen consulate’s refusal to accept local currency for a ship’s bill-of-health fee.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists an August 5, 1940 report by Gourley transmitting revised foreign-exchange regulations effective July 11, 1940 and reporting the refusal to issue a bill of health to the SAN PEDRO MARU, which then sailed for Los Angeles. It also indexes February and March 1941 communications involving Ambassador Grew, the Japanese Foreign Minister, and the Department of State about the consulate’s difficulties with exchange-control authorities. The Department sought to determine whether the incident was a test case or reflected a general refusal of consular services when fees were tendered in local currency; a March 25 telegram concluded that the consul had acted properly. A further March 18 entry refers to the Department’s Division of International Commerce, but its subject is not described on the sheet.

interest: The sheet is useful for reconstructing a sequence of diplomatic papers that are not themselves present in the supplied file text. It exposes how exchange controls in Japanese-administered Dairen created a practical dispute over consular fees and maritime public-health documentation, while also revealing that officials considered the episode a possible test of American authority. The SAN PEDRO MARU’s departure without a bill of health connects monetary regulation, consular practice, shipping, and quarantine administration in a particularly concrete case.
